An afternoon with the Drug Czar

Barry McCaffrey just says " no " to Columbus
by Jamie Pietras

Drug Czar Barry McCaffrey doesn't mince words when it comes to the drug war.

The four-star general was appointed by President Bill Clinton in 1992 to oversee the nation's $17.8 billion federal anti-drug budget and head the Office of National Drug Control Policy. Since he took the reins, McCaffrey's opposition to the decriminalization of drugs has been as fierce and relentless as his heroics in Vietnam.

So relentless that after California voters approved the use of marijuana for medical purposes in 1996, McCaffrey went on a crusade to arrest doctors who prescribe pot.

Last fall, after New Mexico Governor Gary Johnson spoke to a group of Washington, D.C. college students about the ineffectiveness of the drug war, McCaffrey told a group of the state's law enforcement officials that Johnson should " be ashamed for talking to a bunch of college students and telling them that marijuana use is great and heroin use is great. " Students at George Washington University later said McCaffrey greatly misconstrued the governor's comments.

And even though voters in five states and the District of Columbia have OK'd marijuana for medical purposes, McCaffrey still doesn't see pot as a viable medicine. Ten years from now, marijuana won't even be considered for medical reasons, McCaffrey told students at Columbus' Fort Hayes High School during a speech last Wednesday, March 8.

His roundtable discussion with about 30 students marked the first of two public appearances for McCaffrey last week in Columbus. In the afternoon, the presidential Cabinet member was the featured speaker at a packed Columbus Council on World Affairs luncheon at the Columbus Athletic Club.

McCaffrey is to American drug policy what Alan Greenspan is to the economy, so the languid media reception he received locally came as a surprise. One TV reporter and one radio reporter showed up for McCaffrey's speech at Fort Hayes. At the Athletic Club, only one radio reporter and one writer for the Columbus Dispatch took the time to hear the drug czar out.

Even though McCaffrey spent an hour with the Dispatch's editorial board on Wednesday, the daily newspaper printed only a short, page-three article about his Columbus visit. A scheduled interview with Columbus Alive was canceled the day before McCaffrey's visit--after Alive submitted to McCaffrey's handlers the questions we wanted to ask the drug czar. A public affairs representative said the Alive interview was deep-sixed because of a " scheduling conflict " that was outside of her control.

As he reiterated to the few reporters at Fort Hayes, McCaffrey stands true to his belief that voters have approved medical marijuana largely because of the clever campaigning of pro-legalization advocates--not because concerned voters think marijuana can ease the suffering of the terminally ill.

" The people behind [medical marijuana] are primarily interested in legalizing marijuana, " McCaffrey said. " I think [activists] made a very clever argument that says, ‘Wait a minute, if you get cancer 10 years from now, maybe you'll need marijuana for pain management or glaucoma or whatever.' We say, ‘Wait a minute, let the scientists and the doctors work that out.' "

For National Organization to Reform Marijuana Laws (NORML) Director Allen St. Pierre, McCaffrey's oft-repeated comments are infuriating. St. Pierre's organization lists 24 medical groups--including the American Academy of Family Physicians and The New England Journal of Medicine--that endorse prescriptive access to medical marijuana. The New England Journal of Medicine has gone so far as to suggest marijuana's Food and Drug Administration classification be changed to Schedule II, a move that would allow use for some medicinal purposes in the United States.

Nevertheless, McCaffrey told Columbus Alive that marijuana will never be rescheduled by the FDA. He said most reasonable doctors and parents don't want to see pot used as medicine.

" To some extent, it's all a crock, " McCaffrey said of medical marijuana. " If it's a medical issue, let the [National Institutes of Health] and the FDA decide it, based on clinical controlled trials. But at the end of the day, no doctor is actually hopeful that you can get a big doobie as the pain management device for prostate cancer. "

McCaffrey also warned of pot's potential as a " gateway drug " that leads to more serious substance abuse. He said, " I tell people the most dangerous drug in America isn't heroin or methamphetamines. It's a 12-year-old boy or girl smoking pot on the weekends, because that youngster is 79 times more likely to have a drug abuse problem than one who isn't. "

The " gateway theory, " though, was refuted by the Institute of Medicine (IOM) report on marijuana released in March 1999--a report that was funded by McCaffrey's office.

When asked about the inconsistencies between his public assertions and the IOM report, McCaffrey replied, " Like a lot of things out of committee, [the report] was a brokered deal. " The drug czar admitted the report didn't find a " scientific connection " between pot and heroin use, but that there was a " statistical correlation of enormous significance. "
See
The Boston Phoenix Comments On The Drug Czar’s Position On IOM Report -- Top Notch

After the Athletic Club luncheon, McCaffrey tackled more timely questions with reporters. He offered his thoughts on an issue he's been wrestling with--an upcoming Supreme Court ruling that will determine the constitutionality of hospitals handing police the urine samples of pregnant women who test positive for cocaine. Mothers in South Carolina can be charged with child abuse if their babies are born with traces of drugs in their blood, and some doctors and nurses in that state have given women's urine samples to police without consent, a violation of the Fourth Amendment, civil liberties advocates argue.

Though he fears that some women may avoid routine medical treatment if the Supreme Court deems the practice constitutional, McCaffrey said that danger to the unborn fetus is too great, and he supports the measure.

The drug czar also defended his actions in returning ad time the federal government bought from network television stations in exchange for anti-drug messages on prime-time TV programs like ER and Beverly Hills 90210.
See
NORML Weekly Press Release March 16, 2000

McCaffrey said the agreement with the TV networks was never a secret, and that it was outlined in his National Drug Control Strategy. He said that TV producers were not paid to insert the messages into shows, and that media reports greatly distorted the issue. McCaffrey pointed out that the federal government also declared it would no longer review TV programs, as it had reportedly done under previous arrangements.

McCaffrey also commented on the highly publicized accounts of past drug use among the four major presidential contenders. Democratic candidates Bill Bradley and Al Gore were reported to have smoked pot in the past, and Republican contender George W. Bush dodged questions about past drug use when he was on the campaign trail. McCaffrey said Arizona Senator John McCain, the only candidate who wasn't marred by drug allegations, came of age during a time when drugs weren't as prevalent as they were for the three younger candidates.

Still, McCaffrey said he is sick of the finger pointing. " Stop playing `gotcha' with who smoked a joint in the '70s, " he said. Instead, McCaffrey would like to see politicians and reporters ask candidates what they've learned about the dangers of drug use.

The idea doesn't sit well with NORML's St. Pierre, who's witnessed hundreds of McCaffrey speeches and challenged the drug czar to a public debate numerous times. St. Pierre said, " Unfortunately, the `gotcha' game in the '90s is arresting people and putting people in jail. "

Activists like St. Pierre contend that the debate over the drug war has been all but ignored by the mainstream press. The local media's silence regarding McCaffrey's Columbus visit couldn't be better evidence.
